activities.description: Scientist turns off the vacuum, opens the system to the atmosphere, turns on the manometer, and zeroes it by pressing the 'hold' button.
Scientist attaches a sample bottle to the system, emphasizing careful handling. He closes specific stopcocks to isolate the system.
Scientist turns on the vacuum and monitors the manometer reading to check for leaks. He explains how to interpret the readings.
Scientist demonstrates how to fix a leak by tightening nuts on stopcocks and ensuring the sample bottle is securely attached.

text_to_speech: for experiment 2 a manometer will be used to determine the pressure in the system the reading on the manometer is the amount the pressure has been reduced below atmospheric pressure if the atmospheric pressure is 710 millimeters of mercury and the manometer reads 650 millimeters of mercury then the pressure in the system is 60 millimeters of mercury to zero the manometer make sure the vacuum is off and the system is open to the atmosphere turn on the manometer and push the hold button for 2 to 3 seconds to prevent the transfer of grease and moisture to the sample bottle you will need to use finger cots or a lint free tissue attach the sample bottle to the system being careful to handle it by the stopcock make sure that the path back to the vacuum is open and that any stopcocks that open to the atmosphere are closed turn on the vacuum to evacuate all of the gases from the system when the manometer reading stops increasing close the stopcock that leads to the vacuum check the manometer if the reading is steady there are no leaks if the number is decreasing there is a leak to fix the leak tighten all nuts on the stopcocks and make sure the bottle is firmly attached evacuate the system again note the manometer reading and immediately close the two stop that lead to the sample bottle right down the pressure reading remove the clothes sample bottle from the system and determine its mass on the balance remove the bottle from the balance to fill the bottle with air open the stopcock determine the new mass on the balance to fill the system with argon or natural gas connect the fill tube to the gas tap evacuate the system fill the system with gas to approximately fifty millimeters of mercury below atmospheric pressure repeat the process of evacuating and filling with a gas a total of three times to remove all traces of previous gases

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: For experiment 2, a monometer will be used to determine the pressure in the system.
The reading on the monometer is the amount the pressure has been reduced below atmospheric
pressure.
If the atmospheric pressure is 710 mm in mercury and the monometer reads 650 mm in mercury,
then the pressure in the system is 60 mm in mercury.
To zero the monometer, make sure the vacuum is off and the system is open to the atmosphere.
Turn on the monometer and push the hold button for 2 to 3 seconds.
To prevent the transfer of grease and moisture to the sample bottle, you will need to use
finger-cots or a lint-free tissue.
Attach the sample bottle to the system being careful to handle it by the stopcock.
Make sure that the path back to the vacuum is open and that any stopcocks that open
to the atmosphere are closed.
Turn on the vacuum to evacuate all of the gases from the system.
When the monometer reading stops increasing, close the stopcock that leads to the vacuum.
Check the monometer.
If the reading is steady, there are no leaks.
If the number is decreasing, there is a leak.
To fix the leak, tighten all nuts on the stopcock and make sure the bottle is firmly attached.
Evacuate the system again.
Hold the monometer reading and immediately close the two stopcocks that lead to the sample
bottle.
Write down the pressure reading.
Remove the closed sample bottle from the system and determine its mass on the balance.
Remove the bottle from the balance.
To fill the bottle with air, open the stopcock.
Determine the new mass on the balance.
To fill the system with argon or natural gas, connect the fill tube to the gas tap.
Evacuate the system.
Fill the system with gas to approximately 50 mm of mercury below atmospheric pressure.
Make the process of evacuating and filling with a gas at total of three times to remove
all traces of previous gases.
